title: The Expertise-to-Offer Translation SOP

tools.name: The Expertise-to-Offer Translation SOP (5 Steps)
tools.content:
# The Expertise-to-Offer Translation SOP

**What this solves:** The gap between 'I know I have valuable skills' and 'here is what I charge for, in a sentence I can say out loud.' The reason most niche worksheets don't close this gap is that they ask what you're good at and what you enjoy — and then tell you to find the overlap. That approach was never built to separate genuine expertise from the professional identity a corporate environment trained you to perform as a condition of your employment, often for free. This SOP works differently: it begins with systematic elimination, then excavates the specific layer of your former role that functions as a consulting offer rather than assumed background.

---

## STEP 1 — Strip the Job Title

**Why this step exists:** Your former job title is a container your employer built. Inside it are at least three different things: genuine expertise you developed, institutional knowledge that only worked inside that company, and professional behaviours you performed because the culture required them. Most women returning from a career pause try to build an offer out of the whole container. This step separates them.

**Fill in the fields below:**

**1a. My most senior or most recent job title was:**
> [e.g., Senior HR Business Partner / Finance Director / Head of Brand Strategy]

**1b. The three things I did most often in that role were:**
> 1. [Task or responsibility — be specific, not 'managed projects']
> 2. [Task or responsibility]
> 3. [Task or responsibility]

**1c. Of those three, the one that required knowledge or judgment an outsider would NOT automatically have is:**
> [Choose one. If all three feel like 'anyone could do that,' go smaller — what decision inside that task was yours alone to make?]

**1d. The one that was mainly about navigating my specific company's politics, systems, or culture — and would not transfer to a different organisation — is:**
> [Be honest. Institutional knowledge is real but it is not a consulting offer.]

**✓ Carry forward to Step 2:** Your answer to **1c**.

---

## STEP 2 — Name the Expertise Underneath the Role

**Why this step exists:** What you identified in 1c is still attached to a role. This step detaches it — so it becomes something a paying client can hire you to bring to their situation, not something that only existed inside your former employer.

**Fill in the fields below:**

**2a. The expertise from Step 1c, restated without any reference to my former employer or job title, is:**
> [e.g., 'Diagnosing why a mid-size team's performance has plateaued and restructuring the accountabilities that are causing it' / 'Building a financial reporting process that non-finance department heads can actually use to make decisions']

**2b. The type of person or organisation who would need this expertise — and does not currently have it internally — is:**
> [e.g., 'A founder-led business with five to twenty employees who has just promoted someone to their first management role' / 'A small charity whose board receives financial reports they don't understand and can't interrogate']

**2c. The specific problem they are in when they need this expertise — described in their words, not mine — is:**
> [e.g., 'We keep promoting our best individual contributors into management and then watching them struggle for eighteen months' / 'We produce monthly accounts but no one on the leadership team knows what to do with them']

**✓ Carry forward to Step 3:** Your answers to **2a**, **2b**, and **2c** together.

---

## STEP 3 — The Conditioned-Behaviour Audit

**Why this step exists:** Corporate environments train skilled people to give away their expertise as part of their professional identity — in meetings, in informal advice, in 'just helping a colleague.' When you return to work after a family pause, those conditioned behaviours come with you. This step makes them visible so they stop leaking into your offer as free content.
tools.instructions: Work through the five steps in order, filling in every bracketed field before moving to the next — do not skip ahead.

tools.name: The Career Layer Excavation Worksheet
tools.content:
# The Career Layer Excavation Worksheet

**What this is for:** Before you can identify which part of your career is a consulting offer, you need to see the whole structure laid flat. This worksheet maps the layers of your professional history so that the SOP's Step 2 is working from a complete picture rather than whatever came to mind first.

**Instructions:** Fill in every row. Include roles that felt minor or transitional — the expertise embedded in those is often the most transferable.

---

## Section A — Career Timeline (Fill in one row per role)

| Role / Title | Organisation type (not the name — e.g. 'FTSE 100 retailer', 'NHS trust', 'boutique consultancy') | Years in role | The single most complex problem this role required me to solve repeatedly |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Role 1] | [Org type] | [e.g. 3 years] | [Problem — be specific] |
| [Role 2] | [Org type] | [Years] | [Problem] |
| [Role 3] | [Org type] | [Years] | [Problem] |
| [Role 4 — add rows as needed] | [Org type] | [Years] | [Problem] |

---

## Section B — The Expertise Underneath Each Role

For each role in Section A, answer the following. You are looking for expertise that existed across more than one role — that repetition is what makes it a consulting offer rather than a one-time skill.

**B1. Across the roles above, the type of problem I was brought in to solve most often — regardless of job title — was:**
> [e.g., 'Getting two departments who were not communicating to produce a shared output' / 'Taking a process that was held in one person's head and making it something the whole team could run' / 'Translating what the data said into a decision the leadership team could make']

**B2. The industry or sector context in which I solved that problem most often was:**
> [e.g., 'Fast-moving consumer goods, always inside marketing or brand' / 'Financial services, always on the operations or compliance side' / 'Healthcare, always at the interface between clinical and administrative']

**B3. The type of organisation that most often needed that problem solved — and did not have the internal capability to solve it — was:**
> [e.g., 'A business that had grown quickly and whose internal processes had not kept pace' / 'A team that had a new leader and needed to rebuild how it worked' / 'A function that had to report to a board but lacked the language to do it credibly']

---

## Section C — The Pause Inventory

**What this section is for:** The years you spent outside paid work are not a gap to explain — they are a period in which you continued to develop and apply expertise. This section captures what was happening professionally during the pause, so it does not get erased from your offer.

**C1. During the years I was not in paid employment, I continued to use the following professional skills (tick all that apply and describe how):**

| Skill | Used during pause? | How — be specific |
|---|---|---|
| Project management or coordination | ☐ Yes / ☐ No | [e.g., 'Managed a house renovation across five contractors over eight months'] |
| Financial planning or analysis | ☐ Yes / ☐ No | [e.g., 'Managed household budget through a significant income reduction and returned to surplus'] |
| People or team leadership | ☐ Yes / ☐ No | [e.g., 'Led a school fundraising committee of twelve volunteers for three years'] |
| Communication, writing, or presenting | ☐ Yes / ☐ No | [e.g., 'Wrote for a local publication / ran a community social media account to 2,000 followers'] |
| Teaching, coaching, or advising | ☐ Yes / ☐ No | [e.g., 'Tutored children in [subject] / advised friends on [type of decision]'] |
| Research or analysis | ☐ Yes / ☐ No | [e.g., 'Researched and navigated a complex healthcare situation for a family member'] |
| Other: [Name it] | ☐ Yes / ☐ No | [How] |

**C2. The skill from C1 that most directly connects to the expertise I identified in B1 is:**
> [Name it — this is evidence that your expertise is current, not historical]

---
tools.instructions: Use this alongside Step 2 of the SOP to map the full structure of your former career before you select which layer becomes your offer — takes 20 minutes, saves weeks of circling.

tools.name: The Offer Paragraph Reality-Check Script
tools.content:
# The Offer Paragraph Reality-Check Script

**What this is for:** The moment you read your offer paragraph to a real person is the moment it stops being an internal document and becomes an external commitment. This script makes that conversation structured, low-stakes, and useful — so you get genuine signal, not polite encouragement.

**Who to use this with:** One person from your former professional world who understands the problem your offer solves — a former colleague, a peer from your industry, or someone who currently works in the field your offer is aimed at. Not a friend who will be encouraging regardless of what you say.

**How to set it up:** Send this message to the person you named in SOP Step 5c:

---

## The Setup Message (send by text, WhatsApp, or email)

> Hi [Name] — I'm building a consulting offer in [broad area, e.g., 'HR / finance / marketing strategy'] and I want to test whether it makes sense to someone who works in this world. It will take fifteen minutes, either on a call or over coffee. I'm specifically looking for honest feedback, not encouragement — so if something sounds wrong or unclear, that's exactly what I need to hear. Are you free [two specific date/time options]?

---

## The Conversation Script

**Opening (1 minute):**

> "I'm going to read you a paragraph — it's a description of a consulting offer I'm building. I want to know three things when I've finished: whether it makes sense to you, whether you know the type of person or organisation I'm describing, and whether there's anything in it that sounds wrong or that you'd say differently. Ready?"

**Read your offer paragraph from SOP Step 5 out loud, exactly as written.**

---

**Question 1 — Comprehension check:**

> "Without me explaining anything — does that make sense to you? Can you picture the situation I'm describing?"

*Listen fully. Do not clarify or defend. If they hesitate, that hesitation is data.*

**If they say yes:** "What does it sound like to you — what kind of work is it?"

**If they say no or 'sort of':** "What's the part that didn't land? Don't worry about being diplomatic — I'm testing the words, not asking for a verdict on me."

---

**Question 2 — Market recognition check:**

> "Does the type of client I described — [repeat your answer from SOP 2b] — ring true to you? Do you know organisations or people in that situation?"

*If they name a specific person or organisation, note it. That is a warm lead.*

**Follow-up:** "Is [the problem from your SOP 2c] something you've seen come up as a real pain point, or does it sound more like a theoretical problem?"

---

**Question 3 — Language check:**

> "Is there a word or phrase I used that you wouldn't use, or that sounds like it's from inside a framework rather than from real life?"

*Note every word they flag. These are the words to replace in your final offer paragraph.*

---

**Question 4 — The fee question (only if the conversation is going well):**

> "If someone in the situation I described came to you and said they were thinking of hiring a consultant to help with this — what would they expect to pay for that kind of engagement? Any instinct, even a rough range, is useful."

*Do not anchor them with a number first. Listen to what they say.*

---

**Closing:**

> "This is genuinely helpful — thank you. I'm not pitching you, and I'm not going to follow up asking you to hire me. I'm testing whether this offer is real before I take it anywhere. If you happen to know someone who is actually in this situation and might want to talk to me, I'd welcome the introduction — but no pressure either way."

---

## What to Do With the Feedback

| What you heard | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| They understood it immediately and named a real situation | Your offer is operating at the right level of specificity | Return to SOP Step 5, confirm the paragraph is final, move to outreach |
tools.instructions: Once you have completed Step 5 of the SOP and written your offer paragraph, use this script to read it out loud to one real person — a former colleague, a peer, or a trusted contac

tools.name: The 'Is This an Offer or an Identity?' Diagnostic Checklist
tools.content:
# The 'Is This an Offer or an Identity?' Diagnostic Checklist

**What this is for:** The single most common reason a completed niche-identification exercise does not produce a paying client is that the output is a professional identity — a description of who you are and what you know — rather than an offer, which is a description of what a specific client gets and why they would pay for it. This checklist is the forensic test that separates the two.

**How to use it:** Read your offer paragraph from SOP Step 5 and work through each item below. A single unchecked item means the paragraph is not ready to show a client — return to the SOP step indicated and revise.

---

## Section 1 — Does It Name a Client?

☐ **My offer paragraph names a specific type of person or organisation** — not 'businesses' or 'people who want to grow' but a type of client defined by their situation, their sector, their stage, or the specific problem they are in.

> *If unchecked: Return to SOP Step 2b and narrow until you can name a client type a real person could recognise themselves in.*

☐ **The client type I have named is narrow enough that I could find ten of them** — not 'all SMEs' or 'any organisation with a team' but a specific enough description that I could name three sectors or three situations where this client exists.

> *If unchecked: Ask yourself — if I posted this offer description in a LinkedIn group for [my former industry], would the right person read it and think 'that's my situation'? If not, narrow further.*

---

## Section 2 — Does It Name a Problem?

☐ **My offer paragraph names the specific problem the client is in before they hire me** — not the transformation I will produce but the situation they are living in right now that is costing them something.

> *If unchecked: Return to SOP Step 2c. If your paragraph describes your expertise without describing their pain, it is an identity, not an offer.*

☐ **The problem I have named is something the client would spend money to resolve** — not a problem they would solve themselves with a Google search, a book, or a free resource, but a problem that has persisted despite their own attempts to address it.

> *If unchecked: Ask yourself — has this client already tried to fix this? What did they try and why did it not work? Your offer should address why the previous attempt failed.*

---

## Section 3 — Does It Name a Deliverable or Outcome?

☐ **My offer paragraph names what the client has at the end of the engagement** — a decision made, a process built, a team restructured, a capability installed — not a feeling, a mindset shift, or a general improvement.

> *If unchecked: Return to SOP Step 4c. The outcome needs to be concrete enough that both you and the client could confirm at the end of the engagement whether it was delivered.*

☐ **The outcome I have named is mine to deliver — not dependent on the client doing internal work I cannot control.**

> *If unchecked: You may be describing a coaching outcome rather than a consulting outcome. Both are valid — but they are priced and contracted differently. Decide which you are offering and rewrite accordingly.*

---

## Section 4 — Does It Sound Like You?

☐ **Every word in the paragraph is a word I would use in a real conversation** — no jargon I would not say out loud, no framework language that belongs to a methodology rather than to me.

> *If unchecked: Read the paragraph out loud and replace every word you stumble over with the word you would actually say.*

☐ **I could read this paragraph to a former colleague and have them say 'yes, that is exactly what you used to do' — not 'I didn't know you did that.'**

> *If unchecked: The offer may be too far from your demonstrated expertise. Return to SOP Step 1c and check that the expertise you are leading with is one your professional history visibly supports.*

---

## Section 5 — Is It Ready to Show a Human Being?
tools.instructions: Run this checklist on your offer paragraph from SOP Step 5 before you take it into any public-facing context — it catches the four most common ways a genuine expertise gets written

promise: Follow the five steps and fill in every field, and you will leave this document holding a specific, nameable consulting offer traced directly back to expertise you already have. That offer becomes the first thing you say when someone asks what you do.
howToUse: This is your Expertise-to-Offer Translation SOP — a working document you fill in once, in order, to arrive at a one-paragraph offer description written in your own words that you can say out loud, put in writing, and show to another human being. Work through the four tools in sequence: the SOP is the spine, the other three are the fill-in instruments it calls on. You do not need to have your niche figured out before you start — that is the point of the process.

nextStep.body: The paragraph you have written in SOP Step 5 is the input your first client conversation runs on. Inside the programme, the next module takes that paragraph and turns it into the three specific outreach conversations — scripted at the sentence level — that are your path to your first paying client. Open the programme portal and go to Module 2: First Outreach. Bring your completed offer paragraph from Step 5 with you — you will use it word for word.
